name: Myroslav Skoryk
milestone_by_age_26: Composed the symphonic poem 'Silnee smerti' (Stronger than Death) in 1963 at age 25, a work listed among his notable compositions in the Encyclopedia of Ukraine, while a postgraduate student at the Moscow Conservatory under Dmitry Kabalevsky.
early_history_summary: Skoryk was born into a family of Ukrainian intellectuals in Lviv; his parents were University of Vienna-educated and his great aunt was the famous soprano Solomiya Krushelnytska. He entered the Lviv Music School at age 7 but was deported to Siberia with his family in 1947, returning to Lviv in 1955 to study at the Lviv Conservatory before enrolling in the Moscow Conservatory postgraduate program in 1960.
family_context_summary: Born to a family of Ukrainian intellectuals in Lviv; both parents were educated at the University of Vienna, his father a historian and ethnographer, his mother a chemist. His great aunt was the renowned opera soprano Solomiya Krushelnytska.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents played instruments at home (father violin, mother piano) and his great aunt Solomiya Krushelnytska was one of the 20th century's leading opera sopranos who noted his perfect pitch at age 6 and recommended music school. His grandfather was a folklorist and political figure.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Moscow Conservatory, Kabalevsky mentorship, musical family, Krushelnytska lineage, Siberian deportation
evidence_summary: Skoryk's early path was shaped by a musically rich family environment (great aunt Krushelnytska, parents who played instruments) and elite institutional training at the Lviv and Moscow Conservatories. His deportation to Siberia at age 9 interrupted but did not end his musical education. By age 25, he had composed several notable works including the symphonic poem 'Stronger than Death' (1963), which is listed in the Encyclopedia of Ukraine among his significant compositions. His most famous works (Partita No. 1, Melody) came later, but his conservatory-period compositions established him as a rising composer.
starting_point: Born to a family of Ukrainian intellectuals in Lviv; father was a historian and ethnographer, mother a chemist, both educated at the University of Vienna; great aunt was the famous soprano Solomiya Krushelnytska.
current_position: Died on 1 June 2020 in Kyiv at age 81; final roles included artistic director of the Kyiv Opera (2011-2016) and professor at the National Music Academy of Ukraine; awarded Hero of Ukraine (2008) and Shevchenko National Prize (1987).

trajectory.event: Entered the Lviv Music School on the recommendation of his great aunt Solomiya Krushelnytska, who noted his perfect pitch.
Family deported to Siberia by Soviet authorities; continued music lessons in exile.
Returned to Lviv and enrolled at the Lviv Conservatory to study composition under Lyudkevych, Simovych, and Kolessa.
Enrolled in the postgraduate program at the Moscow Conservatory to study with Dmitry Kabalevsky.
Composed the symphonic poem 'Silnee smerti' (Stronger than Death) and the Violin Sonata No. 1, both listed among his notable works.
Composed the Partita No. 1 for string orchestra, one of his most celebrated works.
Named Honoured Artist of Ukraine and received the M. Ostrovsky Prize.
Awarded the Shevchenko National Prize for his Cello Concerto.
Awarded the title Hero of Ukraine.
Died on 1 June 2020 in Kyiv.

name: Timur Miroshnychenko
milestone_by_age_26: Co-hosted the Junior Eurovision Song Contest 2009 in Kyiv alongside Ani Lorak at age 23, a major international televised event broadcast across Europe.
early_history_summary: Miroshnychenko was born in Kyiv and became involved in television as a university student, joining a KVN student team. His TV career began in 2005 at age 19 when he became the Ukrainian commentator for the Junior Eurovision Song Contest, and he became Ukraine's Eurovision commentator in 2007 at age 21.
primary_early_advantage_tags: National TV platform, Kyiv media center, early Eurovision involvement
evidence_summary: Miroshnychenko began his television career at 19 as a commentator for Junior Eurovision on Ukraine's national broadcaster, quickly becoming the voice of Eurovision for Ukraine. By 23, he co-hosted the Junior Eurovision Song Contest 2009 in Kyiv, a major international broadcast. Family background is not documented in reviewed sources; his early opportunity appears to have come from being a student in Kyiv with access to the national broadcaster UA:PBC.
starting_point: Born in Kyiv, Ukrainian SSR; family background not documented in reviewed sources. Attended National Aviation University.
current_position: Active as a TV presenter for Ukrainian broadcaster Suspilne (UA:PBC); continues to serve as Ukraine's Eurovision commentator; residing in Ukraine as of 2025.

trajectory.event: Began television career as Ukrainian commentator for the Junior Eurovision Song Contest 2005.
Became Ukraine's official commentator for the Eurovision Song Contest, replacing Pavlo Shylko.
Co-hosted the Junior Eurovision Song Contest 2009 in Kyiv with Ani Lorak.
Co-hosted the Junior Eurovision Song Contest 2013 in Kyiv with Zlata Ognevich.
Co-hosted the Eurovision Song Contest 2017 in Kyiv as green room host.
Continued broadcasting Eurovision from bomb shelters during the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

name: Eric Adjetey Anang
milestone_by_age_26: Took over management of the internationally recognized Kane Kwei Carpentry Workshop in 2005 at age 20, continuing and revitalizing the legacy of his grandfather Seth Kane Kwei, the originator of Ghanaian fantasy coffins.
early_history_summary: Anang was born in Teshie, Ghana, into the family of Seth Kane Kwei, the inventor of fantasy coffins. He began helping in the workshop at age 8 and chose to continue the family craft instead of pursuing office work as his family encouraged. He introduced Ghanaian design coffins at the Gidan Makama Museum in Kano, Nigeria, in 2001 at age 16.
family_context_summary: Born into the family of Seth Kane Kwei, the inventor of Ghanaian design coffins, in Teshie, Accra. The family workshop was established in the 1950s and gained international recognition.
parent_family_domain_summary: Grandfather Seth Kane Kwei pioneered the fantasy coffin tradition in the 1950s; father Ernest 'Cedi' Anang Kwei also worked in the workshop. Eric began apprenticing at age 8, learning the craft directly from family members.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Grandfather's workshop, family craft, early apprenticeship, design coffin tradition
evidence_summary: Anang's early path was defined by direct immersion in the family craft of fantasy coffin making from age 8. His grandfather Seth Kane Kwei originated the tradition, and Eric chose to continue the legacy rather than pursue office work. By 20, he took over management of the workshop and began reviving its international reputation. The workshop's existing fame and client base provided a platform, but Eric's own dedication to the craft was the driving force. By age 24, he was acknowledged as 'a model for African urban youths' by Le Monde diplomatique.
starting_point: Born in Teshie, Accra, Ghana into the family of Seth Kane Kwei, the inventor of Ghanaian fantasy coffins; grew up in the compound where the family workshop was located.
current_position: Active as a sculptor and manager of the Kane Kwei Carpentry Workshop; maintains dual residency between Ghana and Madison, Wisconsin, where he was the first Thurber Park artist-in-residence (2019-2020); his work is displayed in museums worldwide.

trajectory.event: Introduced Ghanaian design coffins at the Gidan Makama Museum in Kano, Nigeria, under the auspices of Alliance francaise.
Took over management of the Kane Kwei Carpentry Workshop, determined to revive his grandfather's legacy.
Acknowledaged as 'a model for African urban youths' by the French newspaper Le Monde diplomatique.
Began artist residency at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, leading to ongoing connection with Madison.
Selected as the first Thurber Park Artist-in-Residence in Madison, Wisconsin.
Solo exhibition 'Celebrating Death: Fantasy Coffins of Ghana' at the University of Arkansas Little Rock Windgate Center.

name: Vija Celmins
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Celmins earned her BFA from John Herron School of Art in 1962 at age 24 and a Yale Summer Fellowship in 1961, but her first solo exhibition was at the David Stuart Galleries in Los Angeles in 1966 at age 28. Her MFA from UCLA was completed around 1965. Fame arrived later with her photo-realist paintings.
early_history_summary: Celmins was born in Riga, Latvia, and fled with her family to Germany during WWII, living in refugee camps before emigrating to the United States in 1948. She studied at the John Herron School of Art in Indianapolis (1955-1962), earned a Yale Summer Fellowship in 1961, and moved to Los Angeles to attend UCLA.
family_context_summary: Born into a working-class family in Riga, Latvia; father was a bricklayer, mother a homemaker and child carer. The family fled to Germany during WWII and lived in refugee camps before emigrating to the US in 1948.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; parents showed little interest in their younger daughter's artistic pursuits.
evidence_summary: Celmins's early life was marked by displacement as a WWII refugee from Latvia, settling in Indianapolis at age 10. She found solace in drawing and studied at the John Herron School of Art, but her first solo exhibition did not come until age 28 in 1966. No material, independently verifiable milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Imre Gedővári
milestone_by_age_26: Won a silver medal in team sabre at the 1975 World Fencing Championships at age 24, and made his Olympic debut at the 1976 Montreal Olympics at age 25.
early_history_summary: Gedővári was born in Budapest and joined Újpesti Dózsa (later Újpesti TE) in 1964 at age 13, where he was coached by Csaba Zarándi. He made his senior debut with the Hungarian national team in 1974 at age 23 and won his first World Championship medal (silver in team sabre) the following year.
family_context_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Born in Budapest, Hungarian People's Republic.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Hungarian sabre tradition, Újpesti TE, national team, Budapest fencing hub, Zarándi coaching
evidence_summary: Gedővári benefited from Hungary's deep sabre fencing tradition and the elite pipeline of Újpesti TE, one of the country's top fencing clubs. He started training at 13 under coach Csaba Zarándi and spent over a decade developing before his senior national team debut at 23. His tall, left-handed build (190cm) was advantageous for sabre. By 24, he won World Championship silver in team sabre, and by 25 he competed at the 1976 Olympics. Family background is not documented.
starting_point: Born in Budapest, Hungarian People's Republic; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Died on 22 May 2014 in Budapest at age 62; final roles included Secretary-General of the Hungarian Fencing Federation (1989-1991) and President of Újpesti TE (1991-1996).

trajectory.event: Joined Újpesti Dózsa fencing club in Budapest, beginning sabre training under coach Csaba Zarándi.
Made his senior debut with the Hungarian national fencing team.
Won a silver medal in team sabre at the World Fencing Championships.
Competed at the Montreal Olympics, finishing 7th individually and 4th in team sabre.
Won his first World Championship gold medal in team sabre and was named Hungarian fencer of the year.
Won two bronze medals (individual and team sabre) at the Moscow Olympics.
Won Olympic gold in team sabre at the Seoul Olympics, winning the decisive match in a come-from-behind victory over the Soviet Union.
Died on 22 May 2014 in Budapest after a long illness.

name: Tim Berners-Lee
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Berners-Lee graduated from Oxford in 1976 and worked as an engineer at Plessey and D.G. Nash. During a 6-month consultancy at CERN in 1980 (age 25), he wrote ENQUIRE, a private prototype for storing information using random associations, but it was never published. The World Wide Web was proposed in 1989 at age 34 and implemented in 1990-1991.
early_history_summary: Berners-Lee was born in London to parents who were both mathematicians and computer scientists who worked on the Ferranti Mark 1. He graduated from Oxford in 1976 with a first in physics, then worked at Plessey Telecommunications and D.G. Nash before becoming an independent consultant. During a CERN stint in 1980, he built ENQUIRE, a private prototype that later informed the WWW.
family_context_summary: Born in London to mathematicians and computer scientists Mary Lee Berners-Lee and Conway Berners-Lee, who both worked on the Ferranti Mark 1, the first commercially built computer. His brother Mike is a professor of ecology and climate change.
parent_family_domain_summary: Both parents were computer scientists who worked on the Ferranti Mark 1, providing early exposure to computing concepts and culture in the household.
evidence_summary: Berners-Lee had an exceptional family background in computing (both parents worked on the Ferranti Mark 1) and graduated from Oxford with a physics degree. However, his milestone achievement — the World Wide Web — came at age 34 in 1989. The ENQUIRE prototype he built at CERN in 1980 was a private, unpublished project for personal use, not a material, independently verifiable milestone. No qualifying milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Walter Steiner
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Olympic silver medal in the individual large hill at the 1972 Winter Olympics in Sapporo at age 21, and won the Ski Flying World Championship the same year.
early_history_summary: Steiner was born in Wildhaus, a village in the canton of St. Gallen, Switzerland, and grew up in an alpine setting. He joined the Swiss national ski jumping team in 1968 at age 17 but had little success in FIS events for several years before his breakthrough at the 1972 Winter Olympics.
family_context_summary: Born in Wildhaus, a rural alpine village in the canton of St. Gallen, Switzerland. Family background not documented in reviewed sources; he worked as a carpenter by profession.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Swiss Alps, ski jumping culture, national team, Wildhaus upbringing, ski flying specialist
evidence_summary: Steiner's early path was shaped by growing up in the Swiss Alps, where ski jumping was a natural part of the sporting culture. He joined the Swiss national team at 17 and, despite several years of modest results, broke through at the 1972 Olympics with a silver medal on the large hill at age 21. He won the Ski Flying World Championship the same month. His natural aptitude for ski flying — where he was known as the 'birdman' for his flat, wide flight path — was distinctive. He was later the subject of Werner Herzog's 1974 documentary.
starting_point: Born in Wildhaus, a rural alpine village in the canton of St. Gallen, Switzerland; family background not documented; worked as a carpenter by profession.
current_position: Resides in the Swedish rural town of Falun, working as a gardener; retired from ski jumping competition in 1978 after knee injuries.

trajectory.event: Joined the Swiss national ski jumping team but had little initial success in FIS events.
Won Olympic silver medal in the individual large hill at the Sapporo Winter Olympics, and won the Ski Flying World Championship in Planica the same month.
Won silver at the Ski Flying World Championships in Oberstdorf and set world record distance attempts of 175m and 179m.
Won the ski jumping competition at the Holmenkollen ski festival; subject of Werner Herzog documentary 'The Great Ecstasy of Woodcarver Steiner'.
Won his second Ski Flying World Championship in Vikersund and was awarded the Holmenkollen Medal.
Retired from active competition after several knee injuries.

name: Hong Un-jong
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Olympic gold medal in women's vault at the 2008 Beijing Olympics at age 19, becoming the first North Korean female gymnast to win an Olympic medal and being named People's Athlete.
early_history_summary: Hong was born in Hamgyong Province, North Korea, and raised in the industrial city of Hamhung. She began gymnastics at age 7 at a juvenile sports school, spotted for her agility along with her twin sister Hong Su-jong. She distinguished herself in domestic competitions as a teenager and won a bronze medal on vault at the 2006 Asian Games at age 17.
family_context_summary: Born in Hamgyong Province, North Korea, and raised in Hamhung; the youngest of three children. Her twin sister Hong Su-jong was also an elite gymnast who won gold at the 2006 Asian Games. Family financial background not documented.
parent_family_domain_summary: Her twin sister Hong Su-jong was also an international gymnast, suggesting a family environment that supported gymnastics training. Specific parental background not documented.
primary_early_advantage_tags: North Korean sports system, juvenile sports school, Pyongyang Sports Club, twin sister gymnast, early vault specialization
evidence_summary: Hong's early path was defined by the North Korean state sports system, which identified her gymnastic talent at age 7 and channeled her into a juvenile sports school in Hamhung. Her twin sister Hong Su-jong was also an elite gymnast, providing a high-trust peer environment. By 17, she won Asian Games bronze on vault; by 19, she won Olympic gold on vault at Beijing 2008, becoming the first North Korean female gymnast to win an Olympic medal. She was named People's Athlete at 19. Her career was disrupted when North Korea was banned from international competition 2010-2012 due to her sister's age falsification.
starting_point: Born in Hamgyong Province, North Korea, and raised in the industrial city of Hamhung; youngest of three children; twin sister Hong Su-jong was also an elite gymnast.
current_position: Active as a gymnast; last competed at the 2016 Rio Olympics where she became the first female gymnast to perform a Cheng vault and an Amanar vault in the same final; age 37 as of 2025.

trajectory.event: Began gymnastics at a juvenile sports school in Songchongang District, Hamhung, spotted for her agility.
Won bronze medal on vault at the Asian Games in Doha and made her international senior debut.
Won Olympic gold medal in women's vault at the Beijing Olympics, becoming the first North Korean female gymnast to win an Olympic medal; named People's Athlete.
North Korea banned from international gymnastics competition until October 2012 due to sister Hong Su-jong's age falsification, preventing Hong from defending her Olympic title at London 2012.
Won gold medal on vault at the World Championships in Nanning, performing the two most difficult vaults in the final.
Won silver medal on vault at the World Championships in Glasgow, finishing 0.033 points behind Russia's Maria Paseka.
Competed at the Rio Olympics, becoming the first female gymnast to perform both a Cheng and an Amanar vault in the same Olympic final.

name: Hisao Kami
milestone_by_age_26: Debuted for the Japan national team at the 1964 Tokyo Olympics at age 23, and won the 1964 Emperor's Cup with Yawata Steel; selected to the Japan Soccer League Best Eleven in 1966 at age 25.
early_history_summary: Kami was born in Hiroshima Prefecture and graduated from Sanyo High School in 1959. He joined Yawata Steel (later Nippon Steel) in 1960, and the club won the 1964 Emperor's Cup. He was selected for the Japan national team for the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, debuting against Ghana on October 16, 1964.
family_context_summary: Born in Hiroshima Prefecture, Japan. Family background not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Yawata Steel club, 1964 Tokyo Olympics, Japan Soccer League, high school football
evidence_summary: Kami's early path went through Sanyo High School and then Yawata Steel, one of Japan's top corporate clubs in the 1960s. He debuted for Japan at the 1964 Tokyo Olympics at 23 and won the Emperor's Cup the same year. He was selected to the JSL Best Eleven in 1966 and 1967. Family background is not documented. His career benefited from the wave of Japanese football development around the 1964 Tokyo Olympics.
starting_point: Born in Hiroshima Prefecture, Japan; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Alive at age 84 as of 2025; former player and manager of Nippon Steel; retired from football management in 1989.

trajectory.event: Graduated from Sanyo High School and joined Yawata Steel football club.
Won the Emperor's Cup with Yawata Steel and debuted for the Japan national team at the Tokyo Olympics against Ghana.
Yawata Steel joined the newly formed Japan Soccer League.
Selected to the Japan Soccer League Best Eleven and won bronze medal with Japan at the Asian Games in Bangkok.
Played his final international matches for Japan; was not selected for the 1968 Mexico Olympics squad.
Retired from active playing career with Nippon Steel.
Became manager of Nippon Steel, a position he held until 1983 and again from 1987 to 1989.

name: Boris Mikhailov
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Mikhailov trained as an engineer and worked at a factory, teaching himself photography on the side. His first exhibition came at the end of the 1960s (around age 30), and he was fired from his factory job in 1969 after the KGB found nude photographs, which catalyzed his full-time photography career. Fame arrived later with the Hasselblad Award and international exhibitions.
early_history_summary: Mikhailov was born in Kharkiv, Ukraine, and trained as an electromechanical engineer at the Kharkiv Institute of Communal Construction, graduating in 1962. He worked at a factory and used its darkroom to teach himself photography. In the mid-1960s he joined a photo club, but his first exhibition and full-time photography career came after 1968.
family_context_summary: Born in Kharkiv, Ukraine to a Ukrainian father and Ukrainian-Jewish mother. Grew up during the post-Holodomor years and WWII; one of his earliest memories is fleeing Kharkiv with his mother before German troops invaded in 1941.
evidence_summary: Mikhailov's early life was shaped by growing up in wartime Soviet Ukraine. He trained as an engineer and worked at a factory, teaching himself photography using the factory darkroom. By age 26 (1964), he was still working as an engineer with no public photography exhibitions or recognition. His first exhibition came around 1968-1969 at age 30, and his full-time photography career began after being fired in 1969. No material milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Vladimir Yengibaryan
milestone_by_age_26: Won gold at the 1953 European Amateur Boxing Championships in Warsaw at age 21, becoming the first Soviet boxer to win a European title, and won Olympic gold at the 1956 Melbourne Olympics at age 24.
early_history_summary: Yengibaryan was born in Yerevan, Armenian SSR, the fourth child of a teacher and a laborer. He took up boxing in 1946 at age 14, training first with Artyom Arutyunov and then Edward Aristakesyan. He won bronze at the 1951 Soviet Championships at age 19, joined the Soviet national team in 1952, and became the first Soviet European boxing champion in 1953.
family_context_summary: Born in Yerevan, Armenian SSR, the fourth child in the family. His mother Arusyak Mushegovna was a teacher and his father Nikolai Hovhannesovich was a laborer. Modest family background.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; parents were a teacher and a laborer with no known boxing connection.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Arutyunov and Aristakesyan coaching, Trudovye Rezervy club, Soviet national team, Yerevan boxing scene
evidence_summary: Yengibaryan came from a modest family in Yerevan (mother a teacher, father a laborer) and started boxing at 14 under coaches Artyom Arutyunov and then Edward Aristakesyan. He joined the Trudovye Rezervy sports club and the Soviet national team pipeline, winning his first Soviet Championship bronze at 19. At 21, he became the first Soviet boxer to win European gold (1953). By 24, he won Olympic gold at Melbourne 1956. His sustained coaching from two dedicated trainers was a key early advantage.
starting_point: Born in Yerevan, Armenian SSR, the fourth child; mother was a teacher and father a laborer, a modest working-class family.
current_position: Died on 1 February 2013 in Los Angeles, California at age 80; final role was boxing coach in Los Angeles after emigrating from Armenia in 1992.

trajectory.event: Took up boxing in Yerevan, training first with Artyom Arutyunov and then Edward Aristakesyan.
Won bronze medal in the bantamweight division at the Soviet Championships.
Won gold at the European Boxing Championships in Warsaw, becoming the first Soviet boxer to win a European title.
Won his first Soviet national title in the light-welterweight division.
Won Olympic gold medal in light-welterweight at the Melbourne Olympics; named Honoured Master of Sports of the USSR.
Won gold at the European Boxing Championships in Prague.
Won his third European Championship gold medal in Luzern.
Competed at the Rome Olympics as favorite but lost in the quarterfinals to Marian Kasprzyk; retired with 255 wins from 267 bouts.
Died on 1 February 2013 in Los Angeles, where he had worked as a boxing coach since emigrating in 1992.

name: Fujio Akatsuka
milestone_by_age_26: His gag manga series 'Nama-chan' became a hit in 1958 at age 23, published in Manga King magazine and establishing him as a specialist in comic manga, leading to his career as the 'King of Gag Manga'.
early_history_summary: Akatsuka was born in Rehe, Manchuria, the son of a Japanese military police officer. After WWII, his father was sent to Siberia and the family returned to Japan in poverty, living in Niigata and Nara Prefectures. Inspired by Osamu Tezuka's 'Lost World', he moved to Tokyo at 19 and moved into the famous Tokiwa-so apartment in 1956 alongside other young manga artists including Tezuka, Fujiko Fujio, and Shotaro Ishinomori.
family_context_summary: Born in Manchuria to a Japanese military police officer and a former geisha. After WWII, his father was sent to Siberia and the family lived in poverty in Japan; his mother Riyo supported his manga aspirations by providing precious paper and pens.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a Japanese military police officer with no manga connection; mother Riyo supported his artistic ambitions despite poverty. No family domain advantage in manga or publishing.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Tokiwa-so collective, post-war poverty, Tezuka inspiration, Ishinomori mentorship, manga boom
evidence_summary: Akatsuka's early path was shaped by post-war poverty and displacement from Manchuria, but he was inspired by Osamu Tezuka's manga and moved to Tokyo at 19. The pivotal advantage was moving into Tokiwa-so in 1956, where he lived alongside Tezuka, Fujiko Fujio, Ishinomori, and other rising manga artists who mentored and collaborated with him. His first published work came in 1956 at 21, and 'Nama-chan' became a hit in 1958 at 23, establishing him as a gag manga specialist. His mother supported his early efforts with precious paper and pens despite poverty.
starting_point: Born in Rehe, Manchuria, the son of a Japanese military police officer and a former geisha; after WWII the family returned to Japan in poverty, father sent to Siberia, mother supported his manga aspirations.
current_position: Died on 2 August 2008 in Bunkyo, Tokyo at age 72 from pneumonia; final role was manga artist and head of Fujio Productions, established in 1965.

trajectory.event: Published his first manga 'Arashi wo Koete' with Akebono Publishing and moved into the Tokiwa-so apartment with other young manga artists.
His gag manga series 'Nama-chan' became a hit in Manga King magazine, establishing him as a specialist in comic manga.
Began serialization of 'Osomatsu-kun' in Weekly Shonen Sunday and 'Himitsu no Akko-chan' in Ribbon, his first major successes.
Established his own company Fujio Productions Ltd.
Began serialization of 'Tensai Bakabon' in Weekly Shonen Magazine and 'Moretsu Ataro' in Weekly Shonen Sunday.
Won the Bungeishunju Manga Award for 'Tensai Bakabon'.
Awarded the Medal with Purple Ribbon by the Japanese government.
Died on 2 August 2008 in Tokyo from pneumonia after years of declining health.
